I mean, might be one of the biggest individuals I've ever seen in my life. Uh his legs are bigger than me, you know. Um but he moves like like he's 290 or 300. You know, he's a he's a unique blend of size and and speed and movement ability. He's got great feet. Um, so it's it's really been fun just to even in two days see him out working with the vets, see what he can do as far as movement work, see how he's kind of jelling with the other guys up there because that's as much of a of O line play as anything. You know, cohesiveness and and working together. Uh, so, you know, you add someone like that to the room and I already think it's a it's a really good room up front that, you know, you get excited about really all phases, run and and pass game. Like they're critical in in every phase. a bunch of additions on the offensive line, tight end, a quarterback that runs a sub44. What excites you most about designing a run game around the pieces you have this year? >> Yeah, just there's a lot of different ways to attack people, you know. Uh I'd say that's that's the number one thing. And and the cool thing so far is, you know, you watch the guys up front, they enjoy doing drills every day. Again, right now it's not a whole lot of scheme, it's a whole lot of fundamentals. It's a lot of technique. It's a lot of like fitting on combinations. And we're doing that every day we're out here, you know, but they there is no getting bored right now. I mean, they are all about it. They're all in it. Um, they work their tails off. And then, you know, you go to the running backs, those guys are putting in work. Ali's out there working his tail off. Jay Wright's out there working his tail off. Like, guys are really, really getting after it. Um, and then, you know, I think the the other part that's been really fun in the run game has been the receivers. like we've only just scratched the surface of the run game with the receivers, but they they like they want to know it all. They want to make sure that they're involved. They want to make sure that they stand out when when we are running the ball. They're not just pass game catchers. So, I'd say the whole offense, you know, as a whole is is really excited for what we can do. >> What parts of Proctor's game do you think could translate to guard if he settles there? Yeah, like I already mentioned, I mean, he's just a he's a really big human with great feet and good movement skills, you know, and quite honestly, when you do that, you could play anywhere up front. Um, now he played mainly left side in college, so we're going to keep him on the left side, whether it's guard or tackle, you know, he's going to that's that's the bigger transition more often than not. When you start flipping guys sides up front and they're not used to it, that's generally harder than, you know, like tackle the guard situations. I'd say the only thing that changes is it's a hair faster at guard. Uh, and there's a hair more space when you're out at tackle and and that's about the extent of the difference. Um, and you know, he's he's having fun and he's really embracing where he's at right now and and we'll see what that looks like. Really fast, big man. >> Back off, how much? Yeah, I'd say anytime you have a a quarterback who has the ability to run, you know, it's not something that you are going to do down in down out in the NFL, but the threat of it makes it 11 verse 11 as opposed to 11 on 10, you know, and I think I think that's what can get tough sometimes when you get a a guy that maybe isn't as mobile at at quarterback is they have 11 guys and aside from throwing the ball, you're really playing with 10. So, it just lets you equalize some advantageous situations. Outside of that, um really the the mobility these days shows up more in offset situations than it does anything. So, you know, it's definitely a weapon and it's a threat and something you want a defense to think about, but I think no one in the NFL is coming out and just living in that world. >> Jaylen Wadd. >> Yeah, I mean I I having Jaylen Wadd here was awesome. I enjoyed working with him. He was great to have, but I'm I'm really focused on who we have here now. I wish him the best. I think he's going to tear it up in Denver, but you know, I'm I'm really locked in on who's on our current roster. >> You mentioned earlier at this point, it's not about things like that. I'm curious, how do you guys as an offensive staff kind of measure what you have as far as strengths, weaknesses, evaluate where you are? >> I'd say, you know, some of that's done through the evaluation process. So, particularly for young guys, for rookies, you watch so much film, you start to gain uh understanding of, okay, what do we really like? Like, what's this guy elite at? What can we take advantage of? And then maybe what are some areas that we need to make sure we kind of shore up uh and he gets better at? And early on, you want to emphasize what he's really good at. Obviously, uh outside of that, like the veterans that are here, I mean, that's really what this time of year is about. Accentuating your strengths, shoring up your weaknesses where, you know, there there's a lot of times vets can take some big steps this time of year where, you know, you you don't really know what it is you want to emphasize until you get closer into the season. So, I mean, right now, I'd say, uh, everyone's kind of just attacking all the fundamental work and making sure that the core fundamentals we believe in are are at their very best. and then we'll see where it takes us >> with a with a high drafter like Proctor. Are you guys at the process right now where you have identified, okay, this is what this is what really well for us to work on? >> Yeah, definitely. There's things we're working on attacking, but um you know, and there's things probably down the line really for all of them like there it's on our mind. Okay, we got to fix these. We got to shore these up. But it it generally is like, okay, after we get you here to understand this is what we do and how we do it. And they're going to put a lot of time into what we do and how we do it. And as you keep working on that and working on that, you start to get to, okay, here's here's some things that showed up in college. We got to clean this up by the time we get to regular season. Bobby, we want to ask you about something that uh that Greg Dulkich said a couple months ago. He said, you know, everybody's kind of checked their ego at the door. You know, young team and all, I don't know if they want to call it rebuilding, but I wanted to ask what that statement means to you, the checking your ego at the door as somebody who's been here for the past couple years and seen what happened last season. >> Yeah, I think that's really cool. He said that. I actually didn't know he said that. But um you know I I think anytime you want to get better, right? As a coach, you want to be the best version of yourself. As players, they want to be the best versions of themselves. And our job is to help each other do that. The only way you could do that is you got to be able to tell tell the truth, you know? Um like we got to be able to tell the truth to the players. They got to be able to tell the truth to us. Uh it's a two-way street. We got to have real conversations. They got to have real conversations with each other. And so far, you know, early on, I think that's that's been evident with this whole group. All anybody here cares about is growing themselves as much as they can, getting as good as they can as an individual. Uh, and they don't care if it's positivity. They don't care if it's criticism. They want to use it to become better. And I think Greg's a great example of that. I mean, he wants a coaching point after everything he does from anybody. And he just wants it to be the truth. I would say that's that's what jumps out to me.

title: Zach Yenser meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: Tell me about working with Trent Williams and Laramie Tonsel. What does an anchor like that do for the offensive line? And do you need an anchor at left tackle? >> Yeah, I mean both of those guys, I've been very fortunate to be with both of those guys at my time uh with San Francisco and and Houston. Um both of those guys were phenomenal on and off the field. Uh I think both of them were obviously the football aspect speaks for themselves. Uh there isn't anything that they can't do. one-on-one blocks, pass pro, run blocking, all that stuff. But, uh, what really stuck out with me for both those guys was just their leadership in the room. Um, and you can throw Joe Staley in there, too. My first year at the N, like I just I'll never forget like my first phase one with Joe Staley, he was in the front row ready to take notes in his 13th year. Like just that that mentality of just how that run was that that room ran because of that. Same thing with Trent and same thing with with LT and Houston. um uh they just set the tone because of you know they didn't have to say much because of how they played and how they worked. Um and I think it's a huge benefit if you have a guy like that in the room. Um and I compare and I'm not I'm just saying I know it's a different position but like for our room right now like that's that's kind of how Aaron Brewer is in our room like just that leadership role. Um the guys look up to him. He obviously playing really good football and I I put him in that that type of player for our room. question about Kaden Proctor. Um, you know, he would be by my calculation one of the biggest guards in recent NFL history. Jonathan Ogden, the Kai Beckton. >> Why are guys that size able to play guard nowadays? Guards used to be the squatty. >> No, I I Yes, sir. I I just think Kaden just besides the fact how big he is, just his athletic skill set is just I mean when you see how he can move and how he bends. Um that's really what you look at like you know can he just and and again I think he can you know through the whole draft process I think he could play tackle in this league. I think he fits us better and we need him at guard and I think he's going to be a really good guard for us. Um but just those guys that can move the way that you want guards to move. It's not even so much just the squatty bodies, it's just the movement skills really in and especially in this offense, the outside zone type stuff that we're trying to run off the football and and be attacking. Um, he fits that even at as big as he is, he fits that mold. Um, and I think it's it's even more of a plus of how big he is. Um, that that helps us out tremendously. >> And one a followup. So, do the uh when you take a tackle and move him to guard, do the does the pass protection skill translate or >> I mean I I think I think if you move from outside inside I mean I think everything just happens probably a little quicker for him inside. Uh you're not playing with as much space. Um so I I do think like the the the area that you're playing in is definitely smaller. So you got to you got to just understand those set points are a little bit different. Uh you're getting your hands on defenders a little bit quicker. You got to anchor a little better. uh because you are the you're the you know you're the you set the depth of the pocket where the tackles are setting really the width of the pocket um you know inside we're setting the depth of the pocket and and that's a huge part of our protection uh with the timing element with the uh with the quarterback and and understanding where the launch point is and that depth can't be any deeper than you know five yards on on on this drop or it has to be three yards on this drop. Um, and I think that that correlates, you know, you got to have a good anchor no matter what position you play, but it just happens quicker inside.

title: Ladell Betts meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: the the strength of this offense has shifted over the past two years from the explosiveness of it wide receiver room to now the explosiveness and physicality of the running backs. Have you sensed any I guess additional responsibility these guys feel now as kind of the the workh horses of the team? >> Well, I think it's tough to say where the room is shifted. I mean, where the team is shifted because we haven't been out there to play yet, you know. Um, I think on paper a lot of people would assume it's going to shift to the running back room, but there's a lot of lot of time, a lot of, you know, a lot of months, a lot of weeks left before we actually get out on the field. So, we'll figure out a little bit more of who we are and where our strengths lie once we get out there and put the pads on. >> Based on what you saw on tape, what do Ali and Jeremy Wright need to do to take their game to the next level? >> Exactly what they're doing now. Just continue to work. I think the the biggest thing for both of them is to is to get healthy which well they are healthy but stay healthy should I say stay healthy and continue to push because I think when they're healthy they all have a different type of skill set they all bring a little something to the table and the more they can continue to push and the more they can continue to compete it's just going to make each one of them better. So really to me it's about staying healthy and um and continue to compete. >> They're a little bit off message here. You you have a background Coral Springs, Bokeh and Pinerest, correct? Kind of this is a homecoming for you. How how did you get involved in those high schools up there? Did you live here? >> I did. I moved down here in 2012. Uh my wife and I, we kind of left when I retired from football and I and we left uh DC area, we moved down here and this became home. So, uh wife and five kids. Most of my kids were born down here, so this is home to them. >> Nice. >> All right. And and then um when you when you look at this running back room, do you want Devon Han to be the workhorse or do you want him to be the lead back with Jaylen Wright and Ali Gordon making situational contributions? >> I think that stuff will sort itself out when the time comes. I mean, obviously, um Han's coming off a Pro Bowl year, so it' be foolish to assume that he's not going to be out there on the field, right? We he's a heck of a weapon, a heck of a player, so he'll be out there. Um but those other guys are going to be out there, too. In what capacity? That remains to be seen. There's a lot of time between now and and and September. You know, >> I guess to kind of expand on my last question, not necessarily the strength, but Jeff in his intro pressure said, "We're going to run the ball." That's what we want to do. >> I'd love to hear that. >> So, I guess like what kind of mentality does a team need to have when you are a ground and pound team, when your focal point every Sunday is we want to run the ball and push you around? >> I think there has to be a physical mindset. I think anytime you allow an offense to to tee off is and and the reason why I use the term tee off is because when you when you run the ball, you know, we're we're shooting out in terms of offensive line, fullbacks, everybody. So, when you allow a team to tee off, there's a physical mentality that comes with that and uh we kind of get to take the fight to the other team. So, I think when you're talking about a run first type of mentality, it's a it's a it's an attack style. >> Does that almost coincide? Because what we're talking about on paper, obviously, there's a lot of time before results actually happen >> on paper. inside the building. There's not a lot of expectations for this group, just young group rebuilding. So, does the mentality and foc offense of attacking and setting the tone like can you almost do they almost go hand in hand like the underdog mentality and also attacking and setting the tone on the ground? I >> I wouldn't use the term underdog. I mean, that's your term, but I think at the end of the day, this is a National Football League. Um, everybody's here for a reason. No matter what the expectations are, we have high expectations of ourselves. So no matter where we are right now and obviously we're building something and collectively as a group um many of us haven't been together uh long term but we're trying to build something. We're trying to win football games. So attack style whatever it needs to be we're still trying to win. >> Going to ask you about both Jaylen Wright and Ollie Gordon if you wouldn't mind addressing each one as far as things you like about each of their game. Jaylen first. >> Uh Jaylen obviously has some speed. Uh well a lot of speed not some speed. A lot of speed. Um and he's been here I think this is going to be his third year. Uh, so really it's about him staying healthy, uh, continuing to to get some reps, whether it be in practice, but then also in preseason and and try to push the room, you know, obviously we have HN, we have, uh, Ali, and Ali's a bigger back, you know, so he brings a little bit more physicality in terms of just size. Uh, so really it's just those guys getting out there, getting reps, staying healthy, and continue to push each other. >> I think you saw Maxwell at Iowa, right? >> I did. I was there when he first arrived. >> Right. Can you tell us what to expect, what you think of? uh blueco collar guy like most Iowa kids. I'm a little biased. I went to Iowa myself, but um bluecollar um I think he's from Iowa, from the state of Iowa. So I've seen Max when he was probably I don't know 220 pounds when he first showed up to now I don't know what he is, 26, 270, who knows what he is. But Max's come a long way. He's a he's a blueco collar kid. Works hard. It's kind of that Iowa mentality in terms of the weight room strength conditioning program. So he's come up through the ranks and uh you know he's a grinder.

title: Bush Hamdan meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: Being that I think you're in Atlanta, uh Malik Willis is from at the Atlanta area. Did you ever hear about him in in high school? Did you ever Were you ever exposed to him or check out high school football in the area at the time? You know, not not high school football at the time, but just obviously uh you know, with him initially choosing Auburn, being aware of it, and uh so it's good experience to have him here now. Um what are your first impressions of getting to be around him as a quarterback as someone who now seen his potential that obviously has the starting position here. I think so much of it is just uh starting with the human being, you know, there's that factor of anytime you come into a leadership role in the new building, um and just how tremendous a human being he has been. I think he's got this natural knack of knowing exactly who he is and his ability to bring people together. So, I've been extremely impressed with that, the preparation piece, and then uh you know, certainly he's got the skill set uh to to be a really really good player. When you look at what Malik did in Green Bay, obviously it's a very small sample size, but what was something that you saw that he excels at that kind of people aren't talking about enough? I think the biggest thing is just the growth he's had since he's gotten in the NFL. You know, I think we talked so much about it, the expectations you put on yourself as a rookie, and uh so we've gone through it. I think he's battle-tested. He knows what it takes. Uh certainly from his film, uh plenty of arm talent and the ability to extend plays uh are the two things that jumped out to me, and I think uh as his consistency grows, I think he's got a chance to be a very very good player. What's from a leadership standpoint though? I mean, you touched on it a bit, but from a leadership standpoint specifically, what does Malik bring that this team really needs at this stage in the process? I think it's authentic, it's believable. I don't know if you guys have had a lot of time to spend with him, but um he's just as good a human being as you you know, as I've been around in the game, and so I think uh he knows exactly who he is, uh cares about his teammates, not just from a setting of uh it's going to make him play better, but I think cuz he realizes you don't get these opportunities often and so I think he's done a tremendous job of of rallying the guys, all the guys regardless of where they're from, what position they play and and that's been a big thing for us as we start in in this new year. Has there been just to follow up, has there been any specific story or anything that comes to mind that he's done that makes you guys say like wow, this this really is our leader. I know we saw him at rookie camp here last week. I just feel he's always the first one in the building, you know, the last one to leave. I think certainly already in the community he's normally the one pushing you know, to do the right thing and I think guys view him as a guy again who's been battle tested, you know, he's not a first year player, he's been through it, you know, the ups, the downs, has had to battle back. So I just think there's a lot of respect around him and I think that's always such a critical stage with quarterbacks. He's a guy who can who can who can get loose a little bit, break free. Do you guys ever do you encourage that in the in the offense? You just kind of let him be an athlete and do what he thinks is best for a play? Yeah, I think you always want to give him the tools and the structure to get started and then where they take it from there is is obviously it's got to be natural and they got to play fast. I think you know, naturally in this league you can get hit just by playing and so there's always the give or take there of you know, keeping him protected and and that's always part of the balance. What's the biggest thing you're working on offense? There's so many new parts. How exciting is it as a as a coach to see like man, we see this guy's doing something we probably didn't expect. Like how exciting is it to build something from basically scratch is what you guys are Yeah, I think it's exciting, but it's also exciting when you know the guys and you know they've been in the same system for seven years and there's not as much you know, coaching that has to happen, but I think it's always a a unique situation year one again from the staff standpoint of of learning it. Um I think anybody who's being real with players is telling them, "Hey, we're we're doing this together, you know, because it's a new system for a lot of people, um but it's certainly those steps always make this uh this profession exciting." Bush, kind of along those lines, you've worked with the veteran quarterback Matt Ryan and and Julio Jones. Now you're working with Malik. Do you treat all quarterbacks the same in principle or is it different because, you know, different guy, different different circumstance, different experience? Yeah, great question. Um maybe a little bit of both. You know, I never lose um that thought of what Matt Ryan did from a day-to-day standpoint. I don't know if there was anybody I've ever been around uh who was more regimented and and knew exactly what he needed to get done. Um obviously guys like Malik and Quinn are different types of players, uh but there's this obsession I really feel with the great players and uh that's the number one thing for me is is the competition in that room, understanding uh being that that reminder for them of what it takes day in and day out. >> What was your first impression of watching Quinn's film and then meeting him and watching him out here? You know, he's confident. I think that's the number one impression. I mean, the guy um I think that's he's got a lot of starter traits uh and and more than anything, he is a confident player. Sometimes I tell him too confident in some of the throws he makes down field, um but you got to have belief in yourself. It's something that uh you know, Coach Hafley's uh made a priority on this team. He believes he can play and and I think that's his a huge strength of his. And what's the biggest area of growth do you think for Quinn? I think we just want to speed him up at times. He's such a natural thrower. At times it looks like um we got to speed it up, get the ball out of your hands, but I think like anything, um I've been extremely impressed with him and his ability to make all the throws. It's going to come down to decision-making. Uh you know, year one, I think sometimes we can focus on the big plays and the big throws. As you continue to go in this league, it always comes down to the throws you don't make. You know what I mean? And so I think for him, it's year two in the offense. He's got a leg up in that way of knowing it now and knowing what it takes and and just got to continue building. And Bush, I was going to ask you things you like about Gronkowski Gronkowski, the skill set and what struck you about him on his 30 visit. Certainly a guy that, you know, we were we were going through the process with the draft with. Um he's a winner first and foremost. I think we can all get enamored by, you know, the arm talent and what he looks like in the athleticism, but there's just some guys when you put the ball down that can that can move an offense, that can lead, that can win games. He's won a ton of games in college. I really believe he's a guy that, again, has good size, good enough accuracy and arm talent. There's a big jump from college to the NFL as we know and it's been uh it's been a good experience having him out here for the first week.

title: Kevin Patullo meets with the media | Miami Dolphins
text: How much is your experience with Jalen Hurts now helping you uh build the build the offense? Yeah, I think a lot, right? I was with him for 5 years and through different phases of it. And so, I think just going forward from there, just seeing kind of what you can do with a guy like that and how successful you can be, you know, brings a lot. And you know, Malik and I have a really good relationship so far getting, you know, getting to know each other and you know, sitting next to each other in meetings and working through things. So, I'm really excited about it. With the weaponry, obviously everybody's not familiar with one another yet. They have to build chemistry. How do you How do you assist that process? So, really what you do is at this point, right? We want to be as detailed as we can, fundamentally sound, and everybody on the same page. So, it really starts in the classroom, right? As long as we are detailed as coaches and the players can take that from the classroom to the field, that's how you build chemistry, right? You want to be able to throw routes on air, and that leads into 7-on-7, and that leads into team. It's kind of all those little stepping stones that lead to the big moments where when you get a play in the game, hey, we've worked on this so much. So, it really comes down to just understanding the details of stuff and just kind of progressing, you know, through each step. What did you learn from the past year as an OC Yeah, I think really my my all 5 years in Philadelphia, you know, I had such a handle on a lot of different things. You know, I was assistant head coach and then, you know, I was part OC throughout my entire time there. And even last year, I was so heavily involved in a lot of things. I think just the experience of going through that from building, you know, a program up from 21 into this past year, you know, obviously we'll continue to do that. It's just seeing what goes into it, right? When you have a new roster, you're trying to set a new culture in place, you're trying to set a new offense in place, is going through that and what it takes each year to kind of get to that level. You know, we went to two Super Bowls, won two NFC Championships. It's what goes into that. It takes a lot, right? And so, being able to experience that, I think it's probably the biggest thing uh that that I can take with it. And just understanding like it's all about the players, right? You got to put them in a position to be successful. You know, whoever it is, no matter who the player is, you got to do everything you can for them to put them in a position to be successful. So, I think that's the biggest thing. And really right now, what we're doing is is so valuable as far as a staff, getting to know each other as a staff, getting to know the players, and the players knowing us. Just building on those moments so that in critical times in games, we're all speaking the same language, and we know what to do. See a lot of videos this off season of Malik Willis training his mechanics. Just a bird's-eye view getting here to the this for the first year here. What stands out about his work mechanically, footwork, all the stuff that goes into He's extremely detailed in that, right? So, he's he wants to know, which is really awesome. When a guy wants to know more and wants to get him better, and just to say, like, this is what I do, like, that's where you can have problems. But, he really wants to evolve as a passer, know more, and really match up his game with what we're trying to do. So, that's really unique about him, and it's encouraging because every day he's asking questions. He wants to know, "Hey, how do I do this better? Was this good enough?" And at this point in the season, you know, where we're trying to build to those moments, it's awesome. And he is very detailed in everything he does, and you can see just throughout his career he's increasingly got better each year.

title: Justin Peelle: Cade Otton is Always Ready | Press Conference | Tampa Bay Buccaneers
text: anybody asking about shock. What do you like about him? What do you bring to your room? >> Uh yeah, um extremely athletic. Um he's a raw player. He's only been playing the position for a handful of years, so he's still got a lot to learn there, but like his athleticism, like his attitude. Um he's smart player. I mean, obviously he played quarterback, so that kind of gives him a little bit of an advantage, but he's still got a lot to learn about the position and and do like his toughness and his and his willingness to work. >> You got Kade back obviously in your agency and and but you still have other tight ends that that have played, didn't get a lot of targets last year outside of Kate, but what do you see from Kate specifically and how do you see those other guys integrating to Zach's offense this year? Uh yeah, I mean starting with Kade, he does a lot for us. Yeah, maybe the the numbers aren't, you know, up there amongst the I guess the top ones, but he does a lot of things for us that I don't that I think a lot of people don't realize. He does he's really good in the run game obviously. You know, we've had some issues. We've had some injuries obviously at the tackle position and that kind of so we had to do some different things with him to protect those edges and you know unselfish player, team leader on this team does a lot for this team that I think that goes unrecognized and doesn't say anything about it either. just, you know, it's just the guy he is. Um, as for the as for the other tight ends, you know, it was just the way it went last year, you know, um, right, wrong, or indifferent, it just the opportunity didn't come our way. Um, but though again, those guys, and that's what I do love about this room is a very unselfish group, right? They'll do whatever they're asked to do. They don't say anything. They don't complain. They're just trying to help us win ball games. and that and and that's what those guys did last year talking about Payne and then Dev and then Co before he got hurt, you know, and that one it was it was tough losing Co because we lost a little bit of physicality in the room. Um so just excited to have, you know, to see their progresses, especially Payne and Dev [snorts] and then obviously bringing Bower along, getting Co back healthy. I mean, those are all things that are just going to help us win. >> How has Devin Colt grown in the time that he got here? >> Yeah, Dev's done done a nice job with it. you know, he's works extremely hard. You know, it's getting the little details of everything down um in the pass game and in and in the run game and learning to, you know, he's got his process that he goes through and then, you know, what we what we're asking him to do, you know, playing a little bit more of a role on special teams will be big for him. Um, obviously getting him getting him going in the passing game a little bit, you know, and again, it just comes down to details with Dev. He's got the athletic ability, he's got the toughness, smart kid. We just got to get a little bit got to get his details right. Zach use a lot of two tight ends in Atlanta, you know, a good good bit. So, do do you potentially see that a possibility? title: Bryan McClendon on Emeka Egbuka Taking the Next Step | Press Conference | Tampa Bay Buccaneers
text: How's everybody doing? Good. >> Good. Good. Good. Good. I'm ready when you guys are. >> You expected to get a receiver that high in the draft, but I want to ask you about Ted Hurst and just what you like, what he brings to your room. >> Sure. Um, you know, Ted has that that rare size, speed, quickness, all that combination that you have right there kind of wrapped up in one body that everyone I think kind of looks for. Um, and when you start evaluating all the receivers, he was one of those guys that it was like, "All right, we kind of had a range that we could have drafted a receiver." And it was like, "All right, man. Let's just kind of evaluate him." And not really anticipating him being there in that range. And when it all happened, I'm I'm getting more and more excited cuz it was it looked like he was going to be there. And, you know, obviously it was at the top end of that range that we were going to potentially be able to do something with him. And it just it all just worked out where where we were where we were able to get him. And so, uh, you know, just super excited about being able to work with him. Had a chance to visit with him. I know, uh, our organization visited with him at the combine. Uh, I got a chance to get on Zoom with him and talk ball with him and and get a good rapport with the guy and see, you know, just, you know, how he was as a person and, uh, we felt really good about that part, too. So, we're excited about him and obviously has a long way to go and, um, a lot of stuff to learn, uh, in every aspect, but, uh, we're excited to have him here. Coach, what's the the next step for a guy like Abeca Ibuka who did so much as a rookie but really was playing kind of everywhere maybe settles into more of a position this year, but what going to get a lot more attention, right? >> Sure. I think um you know that it'll be good like you said to be able to kind of settle him in at one spot. Um you know Mech uh obviously he's an extremely talented guy. Um he he's an extremely everything you know when it comes to talented, you know, smart, all of that stuff. he kind of checks all those boxes and so uh because he does that you you have a tendency to to use him as much as you can and uh he he got put in a position that quite frankly he was you know we leaned on him probably more than we should have earlier early in his career and uh and it and it was nobody's fault you know guys got hel guys got banged up and you know he was you know he was you know the best guy there and you know so we're trying to do a bunch with him and uh so you know the one to be able to get a lot of the talented guys back out around him that's going to help him out a lot do. Um, and two, he has a whole season of training for for this deal. I mean, I say it all the time. It's really, you know, it's nobody's fault also. I mean, but you got guys that play through a national championship and then they go and two weeks, you know, a few weeks later they're at a combine, a few weeks later they're, you know, they're they're they're drafted and, you know, I mean, a month or two later they're drafted and then a week or two after that they're they're thrown in with the vets and you got NFL off seasonason. So you really never get a chance to kind of heal up from even stuff that you're dealing with as a young player shooting in college, right? And so uh so I think like I said, you know, you had some lingering stuff like that kind of jump up and you know thing, you know, the having to play through 17 games as a rookie. I mean it's just not easy. You know, it's not easy and I think he handled as good as anybody could, but you know, you would like to have been able to help him out some a little bit in that regard, too. >> You have such a deep and talented wide receiver. How beneficial is it for a player like TZ Johnson to get on the field and do some of those things that he was able to do >> in game situations to show you and and your coaches what what he's capable of. >> Yeah. I mean, you you there's nothing like game reps, you know, there's nothing that gets somebody >> ready more than having to get on the line and there are very real consequences on whether you do it right and we win and you screw it up and we lose, right? So, um, you know, guys that are, you know, the older guys have been in those situations a lot, you know, so you can kind of lean on them a lot right now a little bit more in certain situations than you can some of those younger guys. So, um, when when when we got banged up and he had to play, uh, those game reps, you saw him you you saw the trajectory of of him getting better just drastically changed for the better just because he got put in those kind of, you know, life or death situations when it comes to real ball and the real life consequences to doing it right and doing it wrong. And so, um, so the more the most you can get somebody, uh, those reps, you know, the better for them and the better for us. And, you know, we were fortunate that we had a talented guy that we can put in there to be able to get some of those reps. Uh, when we got down on guys last year, >> you mentioned older guys, so much of this offense for so many years ran through Mike Evans. He's no longer here. Um, just what have you sensed from that group as they now have to uh, they all have to step up? >> Yeah. And that's that's what you sense from everybody, you know, it's nobody feeling like that they got to come in here and and try to be Mike, you know, that that is number one thing because you're not going to get Mike. You know, Mike's not walking back through the door. And um and at the end of the day, we know kind of that, you know, that comes with the business part of this the business part of what we do. And so, um, the good thing is, you know, very, very, very fortunate in terms of guys having to have been at that position before where we've had to play a bunch of ball games without Mike over these past couple seasons. And so, uh, so, you know, you do get a sense of, hey, man, you know, how you got to share the wealth and share the responsibility when it comes to being good in the run game, being good in the pass game, and going out there and having to play winning ball at wide receiver. >> How have you seen those guys in that room step up? Uh I mean you know well first I'll say this we got a really good room in terms of just people. Okay so when it comes to just their approach every single day of just how to come in taking responsibility of knowing what to do knowing how to do it maximizing every day maximizing every meeting walkth through and so on and so forth. Um those guys have good habits already built in. So it's not like a jolt in all right man I got to do something extra than more than I have than I have been doing. But just understand right now, man, that just, you know, it may look a little bit different. It may look like we used to do certain out of do do one thing out of one formation that now we we can't use that formation much more anymore because Mike's not here. So, like I said, we've had to live through a couple of those things a little bit before going through these past couple years. And um you know, all those guys are re really fortunate to be in a position where all those guys are older and coming back other than the guys that we just got this this past draft class. just going into his 10th year, which is hard to believe in and of itself, but obviously last year, you know, he's battling through injuries, coming off some serious injuries. >> Now, just talking to him, he just seems like, you know, that's kind of a little bit behind him now. Now, it's about preparing for a season versus that. So, how much better at this stage does he look when he went on the field last year at this time? >> That's correct. It's um anytime you get a full off season, you get to, for a lack of a better term, harden your body up right now for what you're about to come up on right now during that season. And so when you're able to get a full off season and actually train your body up and get your body ready for all those things, um opposed to having just trying to get healthy just so you can be available. Um I mean, it's just completely different. So just when when able you when you able to see kind of the progression of somebody take place more so like right now opposed to being five or six games in you much rather some of that progression being taken place now. And so that that's kind of what he's going through and and uh he's having a great offseason right now like you would expect him to and you know excited to see what he does. >> What kind of threat can Ted Hurst be in the red zone? >> Yeah uh you know it's it's I think you know Ted had let me say this. Ted has a bunch of ability to be able to be a threat, not just in the red zone, but anywhere on the field. Um, and I kind of mentioned it earlier now. He still has a he still has a lot to learn, a long way to go. Um, but ability that he has, man, you know, if he once he knows what to do, knows how to do it. Um, you know, you like guys like that because they could potentially be those mismatches right now, man, for safeties or even corners right now, no matter where you put them. And he definitely has that ability in his body. He still has a long way to go to to get there, but he's definitely has that ability in his body. >> Jaylen McMillan seemed like he was ascending before he had that unfortunate injury in the preseason against the Steelers, but for him to come back the way that he did and I know he's he continues to work in his off season trying to put on mass and with his eating and things like that, just what kind of growth have you seen from him, not just physically, but mentally, especially in in regards to that injury? >> Sure. Um, you know, sometimes you do your most growing through through those dark times, right? And, uh, I think everybody can kind of have an attest to that in some way, shape, or form in life. Um, obviously, man, he had a time that was tough, you know, he had a time that was tough. And like I said, it it was in part because he was doing so well before everything happened. And um so uh I think the growth that he had him understanding one um that it it sometimes it takes some of these dark moments to make you appreciate everything that you got going and and uh the one thing that you see when I say the growth and it's not truly growth but it's just you see that you're really really gratified to see is that um he truly is taking advantage of each opportunity that he gets out here today you know and I don't think he would have had that perspective had he not gone through what he went through. not sitting up or saying he was doing anything wrong or doing anything bad, but you just see him have a genuine appreciation for being out here. And you know, it may be hot, maybe tired days, but you know, it's better than, you know, what he was doing when they had the game taken away from him. So, I think he has a good perspective of everything today. And I think a lot of that is in part to what what he had to go through right now, man, during that time. >> You mentioned Chris and some of the progress that he's made uh this off season. when you look at him, do you still see the same wide receiver who at the start of 2024 he was one of the best receivers in the league? >> Yeah. Well, I think, you know, going into I'll say this, uh, going into the offseason, I think going in every going into the offseason, going into every season, I think it's different, you know, and so, um, you know, be just because your game evolves, you know, the the actual the the the offense has changed obviously, man, we're going through some of that stuff, too. And and, uh, so I I you know, the one thing that we want to do, man, we just we we kind of pick out things that we do well, things that we don't do well. And this is I do this for everybody. and and we kind of go through, we sit down, hey man, you look, you've done great at this. You know, this right here are some areas that we need to improve and we going to improve in all these areas, but I just want to make sure, man, that we kind of know what we're doing well and what we don't. And and kind of going from there and and we kind of did that exact same approach with him. And some of those were the same and some of those were a little bit different, you know? So, we just got to make sure that we're improving on all them areas. And I think I think he'll be I think he'll be just fine. >> With the way that Amecha kind of finished this season, it seemed like he kind of I want to say disappeared, but he kind of faded. how much of that is a function of not being able to settle into one spot, but also, you know, you look at at the receiver room they had at Ohio State and how much the ball was spread around then and then all a sudden he has this period of time where it's like he's the he's the guy out on the field. All the attention is on him and then of course you think about, you know, he's playing so deep into the year because he's playing in the national title game. How did that all kind of, I guess, factor into his >> I think he said it. I think it's a culmination of all that. Um, you know, I don't think it's one thing in particular to say, "Hey, man, this is why this, this is why this." I think when you add it all up, you can see, "Oh, man, I can see how a guy that would go through all that could kind of hit a hit a wall a little bit." And so, um, you know, the best thing that he's had right now, like I said, is an offseason to know exactly what his body's going to feel like and know what to know what to do right now to get ready for it. And so, u, man, he's worked extremely hard right now in that regard. and uh he's a he's able to get over some of the little nicks and everything else that he actually quite frankly came in to the came into his NFL career with. And so uh like I said, nothing major, but just you know, like I said, you start mounting all those things up, it's not easy on him. And um and he handled it as good as anybody. And so I mean, like I said, I'm excited to see where he is. And he's had a extremely great offseason right now. So uh excited about him just in general. >> All right, that's all for Peters. title: Chandler Whitmer’s First Impression of Baker Mayfield | Press Conference | Tampa Bay Buccaneers
text: How we doing? Jalen, this is your first impression of of Baker Mayfield. What do you think of your quarterback? Yeah, I mean, he's fantastic. Um love the scheme that he's in, love the way that that we see the game, and then just the ability to collaborate uh that way, and then also the quarterback position. Mhm. Yeah, I think just kind of personalities are similar. Again, like I said, see the game pretty similar as well. And obviously being both former quarterbacks, there's a there's a marriage there that you kind of have a working relationship that you have to spend those experiences together the same way. I think that's been made very public and and you can see it in his demeanor and the way he operates. It's cliche, Sam, but the guy's a pro already in in the way he carries himself. The fact that he's a guy that it's not like it's just a couple splash plays either. You you hear about his motor. Uh but like all those guys, we sat down in the off-season and talked about three better and three best that we see uh that we can improve. Um but I think some of those main things is just making sure that he continues to stay consistent uh with his accuracy. Anything else? All right, thank you. >> Thanks guys, appreciate you.
